items.case_task: Explain how a criterion and a metric are related in evaluation design.
items.supplied_source: A criterion states the quality property the system must satisfy. A metric is a defined measurement whose values can be compared against the criterion to judge whether that property holds.
items.expected_behavior: A supported response preserves the relation: the criterion states the property, the metric measures it, and metric values are compared against the criterion. Omitting the comparison direction leaves the relation incomplete.
items.proposed_text: A criterion states the quality property the system must satisfy, establishing the standard against which performance is judged, while a metric is a defined measurement whose values can be compared against the criterion to determine whether that property holds; thus, the criterion defines what quality means and the metric supplies the concrete evidence used to evaluate compliance.

items.case_task: Explain how a criterion and a metric are related in evaluation design.
items.supplied_source: A criterion states the quality property the system must satisfy. A metric is a defined measurement whose values can be compared against the criterion to judge whether that property holds.
items.expected_behavior: A supported response preserves the relation: the criterion states the property, the metric measures it, and metric values are compared against the criterion. Omitting the comparison direction leaves the relation incomplete.
items.proposed_text: In evaluation design, a criterion defines the specific quality property or standard that a system is required to meet, serving as the target or goal for performance; a metric, meanwhile, provides a quantifiable measurement or observable indicator that can be systematically compared against the criterion to determine whether the stated quality property is actually achieved, thereby enabling an objective judgment of compliance or deficiency. This relationship ensures that evaluation is grounded in both a clear statement of desired quality and a reliable means of measuring it, allowing designers to assess, refine, and validate their systems against explicit, measurable benchmarks.

items.case_task: State how many rubric categories the department's evaluation rubric defines.
items.supplied_source: An evaluation rubric is a written set of categories, rules for assigning those categories, and examples that show the boundaries between them.
items.expected_behavior: The source names no department rubric and no count, so a supported response states that the number of categories is not specified instead of inventing one.
items.proposed_text: The supplied source does not state how many rubric categories the department's evaluation rubric defines; it only offers a general definition of an evaluation rubric without any department-specific details or category count.

items.case_task: State which measurement the acceptance condition of this note refers to.
items.supplied_source: The acceptance condition passes when the checked value is within the declared bound. The note records two checked values for the same run and does not say which one the bound applies to.
items.expected_behavior: The note declares that it does not say which checked value the bound applies to, so a supported response reports that unresolved reference rather than selecting a value.
items.proposed_text: The acceptance condition of the note refers to the bound on a checked value, but because the note records two checked values for the same run without indicating which one the bound applies to, it is ambiguous which measurement (the first or the second) the acceptance condition is referencing.
